title: AI-Powered Teaching: Literature Review of ChatGPT’s Impact on University Educators
venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT has been used by university educators in higher education and what benefits, concerns, and recommendations have been reported in the literature since ChatGPT’s release. The authors ask which teaching-related functions ChatGPT supports, how educators perceive it, and what risks accompany its use. Their focus is on educator-facing applications rather than student outcomes.

The study is a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020 procedures. The authors searched Scopus and Google Scholar for English-language open-access journal articles published between November 30, 2022 and November 30, 2024, and retained 16 studies for in-depth analysis. The included studies were mostly case studies, experiments, and exploratory surveys conducted in higher education settings across several countries, with university educators as the main users.

Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was reported to support lesson and course planning, creation of teaching materials, development of exercises and assessments, feedback provision, professional development, and ethical guidance. The review concludes that educators generally view ChatGPT positively because it can save time, generate ideas, personalize support, and act as a virtual teaching assistant. At the same time, the paper emphasizes important concerns: inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, dependence on prompt quality, generic or repetitive advice, technical limitations, bias, plagiarism and cheating risks, privacy concerns, overreliance, and the need for human verification and clear institutional guidelines. The authors also note that the evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, so their conclusions are narrative rather than quantitative.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative systematic review of 16 studies, not a meta-analysis, RCT, or rigorously appraised QED. The authors explicitly note the lack of formal risk-of-bias assessment and the heterogeneity of included study types, so the evidence base is descriptive and qualitative rather than high-causal-credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical benefits for teacher productivity and some learner engagement gains, but it provides no pooled effect sizes and no direct K-12 evidence. Reported impacts are plausible and useful, yet remain modest and largely indirect for the requested K-12 teacher-facing GenAI coaching question.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use by university educators for lesson planning, assessment generation, teaching-material creation, feedback, and instructional support in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes 16 open-access studies and concludes that ChatGPT generally saves educators time by helping generate course outlines, lesson plans, assessment items, and teaching materials. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, but repeatedly characterizes the tool as improving workflow efficiency and reducing workload across pedagogical tasks.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported educator uses and perceived workload/time savings

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT is described as supporting critical thinking, analysis, interpretation, and self-regulated learning, especially when used for question generation, discussion prompts, and iterative feedback. However, the paper also notes risks of overreliance, reduced critical engagement, and weak skill assessment when educators use AI outputs uncritically.
finding.measure: Reported effects on critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and self-regulation in the reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights institutional implications such as the need for training, ethics guidance, academic integrity policies, and limits on private/sensitive data disclosure when using ChatGPT. It also flags concerns about bias, plagiarism, cheating, privacy, and the need for human oversight, but does not provide quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Reported policy, ethics, and governance concerns across the reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that educators perceived ChatGPT as increasing student motivation, autonomy, and engagement when used to provide personalized guidance, instant feedback, and interactive tasks. At the same time, it warns that unmoderated use can encourage dependency and overreliance, making the overall pattern mixed in practice.
finding.measure: Reported motivation, autonomy, engagement, and dependency concerns in qualitative/experimental studies
